basic_identification.name: Archival gap for born-digital works
basic_identification.originator: Systemic failure across institutions. Partial responses from Rhizome (ArtBase, Webrecorder/Conifer), Le Random, Library of Congress, Smithsonian, NARA, Yale Born Digital Archives Group
basic_identification.year: Ongoing since the emergence of net art in the 1990s. Increasingly acute since 2021 NFT boom produced millions of on-chain works with no preservation strategy
basic_identification.geography: Global gap. Preservation efforts concentrated in North America (Rhizome, Smithsonian, Library of Congress) and Europe (ZKM, V&A). Near-zero preservation infrastructure in Global South, Asia, Africa

core_ideas.core_claim: The digital art field is producing work faster than it can preserve. No field-wide preservation strategy exists. Born-digital works depend on platforms, blockchains, storage services, and software formats that may not persist. The archival gap is a deep-time infrastructure failure — the field risks losing its own history as it creates it.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Born-digital works face unique preservation challenges absent in traditional media: software dependency (works break when browsers, operating systems, or plugins update), platform dependency (works hosted on centralized platforms disappear when platforms close), chain dependency (NFTs depend on blockchain infrastructure and IPFS/Arweave pinning), format obsolescence (proprietary formats become unreadable), and interactivity (preserving behavior, not just appearance, requires emulation or migration).
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The attention economy actively works against preservation. Platforms optimize for new content, not archival access. Social media algorithms bury older work. NFT marketplaces prioritize trending collections over historical significance. The economic incentives are entirely misaligned with long-term preservation — attention accrues to the new, not the enduring.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Preservation is deeply intention-aligned. It serves the long-term structural needs of the field (maintaining its history, enabling future scholarship, preserving artistic legacy) rather than capturing engagement. The gap represents a fundamental failure of intentional infrastructure — the field has built market infrastructure but not memory infrastructure.

market_economics.revenue_model: Preservation has no revenue model. Rhizome operates on grants (Mellon Foundation, NEA) and institutional support (New Museum affiliation). Le Random is venture-funded with permanent capital structure. Smithsonian and NARA are government-funded. No market mechanism funds preservation. The costs are real (storage, emulation development, staff time) but no buyer or collector directly pays for archival access.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure — entirely outside the market value chain. Preservation creates long-term cultural value but generates no transactional revenue.
market_economics.price_range: Not applicable — preservation is a cost center, not a revenue-generating activity. Rhizome's Preservation Services program provides consulting and conservation services to institutions but pricing is not publicly disclosed.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Stable to growing. Rhizome launched formal Preservation Services in August 2024. Le Random continues building its permanent collection. Institutional interest in born-digital preservation is growing through conferences (DigiCAM25 at University of London, Archiving 2025). But the gap between production volume and preservation capacity continues to widen.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Not applicable directly. However, collectors have a latent stake in preservation — their holdings lose value if the underlying works become inaccessible. High-net-worth collectors of digital art are beginning to recognize this risk.
market_economics.sustainability: Extremely fragile. Preservation requires perpetual funding — unlike a one-time purchase, digital preservation demands ongoing storage costs, software maintenance, and format migration. No self-sustaining model exists. Rhizome's 15-year track record is exceptional but depends on continued philanthropic support. The Smithsonian has institutional permanence but limited digital art focus. Most preservation efforts could collapse if a single funding source withdraws.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Key preservation tools: Rhizome Conifer (web archiving), Webrecorder (browser-based archiving), Emulation-as-a-Service (running legacy software), IPFS and Arweave (decentralized storage), Wikibase/Linked Open Data (metadata management). File format standards: OAIS reference model, PREMIS metadata, Dublin Core. Blockchain-specific: on-chain storage, IPFS pinning services, Arweave permaweb.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI could potentially assist preservation through automated format detection, migration path recommendation, and metadata extraction. However, AI-generated art creates additional preservation challenges — prompts, model weights, training data, and generation parameters are part of the work but rarely preserved alongside outputs. No established standard for preserving AI art provenance exists.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: The preservation gap is most acute for live, interactive, and generative works. Static images and videos can be preserved using established techniques. But works that involve real-time computation, user interaction, network connections, or evolving generative processes require fundamentally different approaches (emulation, re-implementation) that are technically complex and expensive.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: The vocabulary for discussing digital art preservation is borrowed from library science and archival studies (bit-level preservation, migration, emulation, fixity). It lacks art-specific language for describing what is lost when a work is partially preserved — the aesthetic, experiential, and relational dimensions of loss are not captured by technical preservation terminology.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Commons over capture (preservation is inherently a commons activity). Infrastructure over spectacle (archiving is invisible work). Openness over enclosure (Rhizome's tools are open-source). Collective over individual (preservation serves the field, not individual market interests).

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mixed. Rhizome's tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) are open-source. The ArtBase uses Linked Open Data via Wikibase. NARA publishes its Digital Preservation Framework on GitHub. But many institutional preservation systems are proprietary. On-chain storage (IPFS, Arweave) is open infrastructure but depends on economic incentives (pinning costs, token economics) for persistence.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Fragmented. No single governing body for born-digital art preservation. Each institution makes independent decisions. Rhizome leads through technical innovation. NARA and Library of Congress set government standards. No equivalent of ICOM (International Council of Museums) specifically for digital art preservation.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Critical issue. Artists often lose control of their work's preservation. Platform-hosted works are preserved (or not) at the platform's discretion. On-chain works depend on blockchain and storage layer persistence. Rhizome's ArtBase preserves works with artist consent but artists cannot self-serve. No standard for artist-controlled preservation exists.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low across the field. Different institutions use different metadata standards, storage systems, and preservation approaches. Rhizome's use of Linked Open Data and Wikibase is an exception that enables interoperability. No universal standard connects institutional archives, on-chain metadata, and marketplace records.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: This IS the preservation strategy gap. Partial strategies exist: Rhizome (emulation, web archiving, LOD), Smithsonian (bit-level preservation, migration, emulation), on-chain community (IPFS, Arweave). But no field-wide strategy coordinates these efforts or addresses the scale of the problem.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Largely absent. Works are preserved or not without standardized consent mechanisms. Artists cannot specify preservation preferences in machine-readable form. No opt-in/opt-out framework for inclusion in archives. Rhizome's ArtBase accepts submissions but the process is manual and curatorial, not consent-architected.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The traditional art world has centuries of preservation infrastructure (museums, climate-controlled storage, conservation labs). Born-digital art has almost none of this. Institutional absorption of digital art (e.g., museums acquiring NFTs) does not solve the problem because museums lack technical preservation capacity for software-based works.
field_position.what_it_enables: When functional, preservation enables: art historical scholarship, exhibition of historical works, understanding of artistic lineage and influence, protection of cultural heritage, and long-term value maintenance for collectors.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Field-wide coordination. Standardized metadata for preservation. Artist-controlled preservation mechanisms. Preservation infrastructure for interactive and generative works. Economic models to fund perpetual preservation. Integration between on-chain provenance and institutional archives. Preservation infrastructure for works on non-Ethereum chains (Tezos, Solana, etc.).
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists on smaller or less-established blockchains. Artists whose work depends on centralized platforms that may close. Artists without institutional connections who cannot access Rhizome or museum preservation programs. Artists in the Global South where no preservation infrastructure exists. Artists working in ephemeral or performance-based digital media.
field_position.frontier_signal: Established as a recognized problem but frontier as a solution space. Rhizome's 2024 Preservation Services launch and the growth of Emulation-as-a-Service represent frontier infrastructure. The challenge of preserving AI-generated art is entirely frontier territory with no established approaches.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Institutional channels, academic conferences (DigiCAM25, Archiving 2025), specialist publications. Preservation work is largely invisible to the broader art world and public. Discovery is limited to those already embedded in preservation communities.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Very low attention dependency. Preservation work continues regardless of public attention. However, funding for preservation depends partly on public awareness of the problem, creating a paradox: the work is invisible by nature but needs visibility to secure resources.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-aligned. Preservation serves the deepest structural need of any cultural field: maintaining access to its own history. This is pure infrastructure work with no attention-capture component.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Potentially the highest commons contribution of any activity in the field. Preserved works become part of shared cultural heritage. Open-source tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) contribute to preservation commons. Linked Open Data approaches enable interoperable knowledge. But the contribution is unrealized at scale due to the infrastructure gap.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: The gap affects both ownership and meaning provenance. On-chain provenance tracks ownership but not context, interpretation, or significance. Institutional archives track some meaning provenance (exhibition history, critical reception) but this is not linked to on-chain records. The preservation gap means both types of provenance are at risk of loss.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical. Preservation operates on a timescale of decades to centuries. The gap is between the field's production tempo (real-time, continuous) and its preservation tempo (near-zero for most works). This temporal mismatch is the core structural failure.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: This item IS about absence — the systematic loss of born-digital works over time. The gap detects absence (we know works are being lost) but cannot address it at scale. No mechanism exists to even inventory what has already been lost.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Neither. Preservation approaches are fragmented without shared principles. Different institutions prioritize different aspects (Rhizome emphasizes access, Smithsonian emphasizes bit-level integrity, on-chain community emphasizes permanence through decentralization). No coherence framework connects these approaches.
coherence.contestability: Low. Preservation decisions (what to preserve, how to preserve it, what fidelity is acceptable) are made by individual institutions without external review or challenge mechanisms. Artists cannot contest how their work is preserved or whether it is preserved at all.
coherence.forkability: Moderate. Open-source tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) can be forked and deployed independently. But preservation requires ongoing institutional commitment, not just software — forking the tools does not fork the organizational capacity to maintain archives over decades.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: A(DAI) should adopt the principle that intelligence infrastructure must include preservation by design, not as an afterthought. Every signal, node, and relationship in A(DAI) should be durably stored with preservation metadata. A(DAI) should learn from Rhizome's Linked Open Data approach (Wikibase) for interoperable, machine-readable preservation. A(DAI) should also learn from the LOCKSS principle (Lots of Copies Keep Stuff Safe) and build redundancy into its storage architecture.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: A(DAI) should refuse platform-dependent storage without fallback. It should refuse to build on any single storage layer (IPFS alone, a single cloud provider) without redundancy. It should refuse the assumption that blockchain permanence equals preservation — on-chain data persists but may become inaccessible without context, tooling, and maintained interfaces.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) operates at the level of meaning and context; preservation infrastructure operates at the level of bits and formats. The tension is between preserving the physical artifact (the file, the code, the blockchain record) and preserving the meaning (the context, the interpretation, the relational significance). A(DAI) could bridge this by building meaning-layer preservation alongside bit-level preservation.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Copyright law complicates preservation. Making copies for archival purposes may require specific legal exemptions. The US Copyright Act Section 108 provides limited library and archive exceptions. EU Copyright Directive includes preservation exceptions but implementation varies by member state. DMCA anti-circumvention provisions can prevent preservation of DRM-protected works. No specific regulation addresses on-chain art preservation.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Complex. Preservation requires copying, which implicates copyright. Institutional archives typically operate under fair use or specific legal exemptions. On-chain works have varied IP terms (some CC0, some all-rights-reserved). No standardized IP framework for digital art preservation exists.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Mostly opt-in for institutional programs (artists submit to Rhizome ArtBase). Opt-out is the default for on-chain works — they are publicly visible but not actively preserved unless someone takes action. No mechanism for artists to signal preservation preferences.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: High and dangerous. Works hosted on centralized platforms (galleries, marketplaces, social media) are entirely dependent on those platforms' continued operation and preservation decisions. Works on IPFS depend on pinning services continuing to operate. Works on Arweave depend on the Arweave network's long-term viability. Even on-chain works depend on blockchain infrastructure remaining accessible.
ecosystem.network_effects: Negative network effects for preservation. As more works are produced, the preservation backlog grows. Each new platform, chain, or format creates additional preservation complexity. The network effect of production works against the capacity for preservation.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The 2022-2023 crash exposed preservation vulnerabilities. Platforms that closed (e.g., various NFT marketplaces) took hosted metadata and media with them. IPFS-hosted works with unpaid pinning became inaccessible. The crash demonstrated that market infrastructure is not preservation infrastructure. Post-crash: growing institutional awareness of the problem, Rhizome's 2024 Preservation Services launch, Le Random's permanent collection model, but the gap continues to widen.
